title: FACTORIES OF RESILIENCE: How AI is changing the role of schools with Julian Fisher
description: Send us Fan Mail In part two of a three episode deep dive into the education industry, discover how AI can revolutionise learning by providing customised experiences and alleviating teachers' burdens, allowing them to focus on what truly matters—igniting creativity and fostering meaningful connections. Guest Julian Fisher, founder and CEO of Venture Education, lends his unique insights from his journey in international schooling, highlighting the balance between technology and human touch in cultivating resilient, well-rounded students. In the shadow of a rapidly changing and uncertain future should the focus of schools be on creating a more resilient generation of children? Ever wondered if AI could shift education from job training to life skills? Let's delve into this fascinating possibility, emphasising the irreplaceable role of human teachers in fostering emotional and social growth. Drawing from the Montessori model, we explore how AI can complement, rather than replace, human interaction in education, preparing students not just for careers but for life. Julian's experiences in China provide a window into how different educational institutions are embracing AI, from minimal use to full integration, shedding light on both the promise and pitfalls of this technology. Is technology the future or a threat to traditional education methods? We weigh the benefits of AI in easing administrative loads against the risks of over-reliance, especially in tasks like essay writing. As we reflect on the slow technological adoption in education, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, we underscore the need for a cautious yet optimistic approach. The importance of resilience in the digital age, practical strategies to balance tech use, and the evolving landscape of performance assessment are all thoughtfully examined. Join us as we navigate these complexities, ensuring a balanced and enriched learning environment for future generations. On Exactitude in Science: Borges.pdf (kwarc.info) Venture Education | Empowering Education in China
summary: Part two of the education series: Jimmy and Matt chew over AI in classrooms before interviewing Julian Fisher, co-founder of education consultancy Venture Education in Beijing. Fisher argues schools are becoming factories of resilience rather than transferrers of skills, warns we overestimate AI short-term and underestimate it long-term, and recommends Borges' one-page parable On the Exactitude of Science as the perfect lens on AI-era knowledge.
keyTalkingPoints: Fisher's research categories schools into minimal, tokenistic, integrated and embedded AI adoption — even the best are not truly integrated yet
Teachers adopted AI first for lesson plans, marking and admin; students followed, less wisely, plugging in essay prompts
The AI-counselling paradox: once you understand the process, counselling is replicable — and humans may pay a premium for handmade craft skills like guitar or furniture
Fisher worries about AI talking to AI — CVs written by AI screened by AI — and bad-data-in, bad-data-out in market intelligence work
US universities are pushing portfolio-based assessment because essays can no longer prove anything

jimmy: He is optimistic about education specifically — huge opportunities even if jobs for kids in 10-20 years are uncertain
Teaching will not lose jobs imminently because it needs the human touch; tailoring to six kids at a glance is beyond foreseeable AI
Superintelligence will happen at some point, but it will not be a large language model
AI should free teachers from lesson-planning drudgery they hate
matt: AI in education will augment teachers — removing marking and planning burdens so they can do the interaction they value
We overestimate AI's short-term impact and underestimate its long-term impact, and education moves slowly
Schools must teach AI use and critical thinking — parents have a veto through their expectations
He is worried about the dead-internet effect: half of online data could be AI-generated within a year or two
